h1: Wireless Vertical Mice Worth Buying in 2026: 8 Picks, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Wireless Vertical Mice: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 wireless vertical mice compared on dongle versus Bluetooth, battery type, hand size and buttons, from budget to premium.
summary: The Logitech MX Vertical is the wireless vertical mouse to get when you want both a dongle and Bluetooth, since it pairs with several devices and recharges instead of eating batteries. The Logitech Lift suits smaller hands, the Razer Pro Click V2 adds six programmable buttons, and the Lekvey and ProtoArc are the budget rechargeables for a single desk.
intro: Going wireless with a vertical mouse hides a choice most listings do not spell out: do you want a dongle, Bluetooth, or both? A dongle mouse is dead simple but eats a USB port, which is a real problem on thin laptops. Bluetooth frees the port but can be slower to wake, and it only becomes valuable if you have more than one device to pair.

We ranked these eight by how well their wireless setup matches real desks. The review draws on the listings and spec sheets for connection type, battery design, body size, button count and price bucket. Nothing here is based on bench measurements, so where a range or lag figure is not published we leave it out.

products.name: Logitech MX Vertical Wireless Mouse Ergonomic Design
products.verdict: Pick a dongle or Bluetooth, pair several machines and never buy a battery.
products.description:
The MX Vertical gives you a choice of wireless link: either a 2.4GHz receiver or Bluetooth. It adds multi-device pairing through Logitech software and a rechargeable internal battery, wrapped in a premium shell.

It tops the list because the dual link is the whole reason to buy wireless in the first place. A dongle keeps the connection steady for a main workstation, and Bluetooth lets the same mouse hop to a second laptop or tablet. None of the other mice here offer that combination at this build level except the Lift, which trades size for a gentler pitch.

Buy it if you want one mouse for a desktop and a laptop. The caveat is bulk: the body is full size and the price bracket is the highest in the ranking.
pros: Choose dongle or Bluetooth as needed
Pairs with more than one device
Charges over USB, no spare cells
Sturdy premium shell feels durable
cons: Costs the most of the eight
products.idealFor: People who split time between a desktop and a laptop.
products.skipIf: You have a small hand or a tight budget.

products.name: Logitech Lift Vertical Ergonomic Wireless Mouse
products.verdict: The same two-way wireless flexibility in a smaller shell for smaller hands.
products.description:
The Lift is a compact vertical mouse offering the same dual link as the MX, with a dongle or Bluetooth, plus multi-device software and a rechargeable battery. It sits at the mid-to-premium end of the price scale, in the $50 to $100 bucket.

It finishes second since its main appeal is fit. Average and smaller hands often struggle with a full-size vertical body, and the Lift solves that without sacrificing connectivity. Compared with the Razer below it, the Lift is simpler: fewer buttons, fewer learning curves, but more reliable ergonomics for most users.

Choose it if you want Bluetooth flexibility in a body that does not stretch your fingers. If you want a steeper tilt or more programmable buttons, look elsewhere.
pros: Compact shell fits smaller hands
Two wireless modes for multiple devices
Rechargeable battery cuts running costs
Easy shape for first-time users
products.idealFor: Smaller-handed users who need Bluetooth on the go.

products.name: Razer Pro Click V2 Vertical Wireless Mouse, 6 Button Ergonomic Design
products.verdict: Six programmable buttons make this the wireless vertical mouse for macro-heavy work.
products.description:
The Pro Click V2 Vertical is a wireless vertical mouse from Razer with six programmable buttons and a rechargeable battery. The listing treats it as a premium option, priced within $50 to $100.

The extra buttons are what earn it third place. Mapping copy, paste, undo or app shortcuts to thumb buttons can speed up repetitive tasks, and few vertical mice offer that many controls. Against the Lift it has a bigger feature set, but the listing carries a smaller body of owner feedback, so long-term reliability is less certain.

It is a strong buy for spreadsheet, editing or support work where shortcuts save time. Be cautious if you want a track record behind the purchase.
pros: Six buttons can run custom shortcuts
Rechargeable battery avoids AA swaps
Premium brand with software support
Vertical grip with a power-user feature set
cons: Needs software for custom button maps
products.idealFor: Power users who want shortcuts under their thumb.
products.skipIf: You prefer a product with a long record.

products.name: Anker 2.4G Wireless Ergonomic Mouse, Right Hand Vertical Mouse
products.verdict: A plain 2.4GHz dongle mouse that does one job at a budget price.
products.description:
The Anker is a right-handed vertical mouse that connects through a 2.4GHz USB dongle and runs on AA batteries. It sits in the under $25 bracket, which makes it one of the cheapest ways into a wireless vertical design.

It ranks fourth because it is dependable but dated: AA cells need swapping, there is no Bluetooth and it only suits right hands. In its favor, dongle connections tend to be steady, and a standard AA battery is available anywhere if you run out mid-day.

Buy it if you have one computer and a spare USB port and want to spend very little. Skip it if you are left-handed or want to pair a second device.
pros: Cheap entry to wireless vertical use
Dongle link is steady and simple
AA cells are easy to find anywhere
Known brand behind a budget model
cons: No Bluetooth for a second device
products.idealFor: Right-handed users with one PC and a limited budget.
products.skipIf: You want a rechargeable or Bluetooth mouse.

products.name: Lekvey Ergonomic Mouse, Rechargeable Vertical Wireless Mouse
products.verdict: Rechargeable, single-device and cheap, for a desk that never changes computers.
products.description:
The Lekvey is a budget vertical mouse with a rechargeable internal battery and a 2.4GHz dongle. The listing makes clear it pairs with a single device, which is why it can stay in the under $25 bucket.

It ranks fifth because it is an honest, narrow product. If you only ever use one computer, it saves you from paying for Bluetooth you will not use and from replacing AA cells. Against the ProtoArc it offers a mid-size body rather than a compact one, so it suits average hands better than small ones.

Choose it for a home office with one PC. Skip it if you switch between machines.
pros: Rechargeable battery at a bargain price
Dongle pairing is quick and stable
Mid-size shell suits average hands
Skips features you may never use
cons: Little detail on tilt in listing
products.idealFor: Home-office users with a single computer.
products.skipIf: You carry a laptop and a desktop.

products.name: ProtoArc EM11 NL Wireless Ergonomic Vertical Mouse, Rechargeable
products.verdict: A small, rechargeable dongle mouse for people who find vertical mice too big.
products.description:
The EM11 NL pairs a small vertical shell with a rechargeable battery and a 2.4GHz dongle. The listing calls out single-device pairing, and the price lands in the budget-to-mid range.

It takes sixth place because the compact shell is its main attraction and its main limit. Small hands will like the fit; large hands will feel cramped. It beats the Anker for convenience since there are no AA cells, but lacks the Lift's Bluetooth.

This is the pick for small hands on a single computer. Look elsewhere if your hand is large.
pros: Compact shape suits smaller hands
Recharges without buying batteries
Dongle needs no pairing procedure
Budget-friendly rechargeable model
products.skipIf: You have large hands or several computers.

products.name: Luhaso Ergonomic Vertical Wireless Mouse, 57 degree, Small/Medium Hands
products.verdict: Sized openly for small to medium hands, with a stated 57-degree tilt.
products.description:
The Luhaso says in its title that it targets small to medium hands and states a 57-degree tilt, which is rare candor among budget mice. It connects wirelessly and sits in the under $25 bucket.

It ranks seventh because the listing leaves out details such as battery type and whether Bluetooth is included, so it is hard to compare on equal terms with the picks above. The upside is clarity about the hand size it is built for, which saves returns.

It is a fair buy for smaller hands that want a steeper stated angle on a tiny budget. Confirm the battery and link type on the product page before ordering.
pros: Stated 57-degree angle is easy to judge
Sized plainly for smaller hands
Budget price with little financial risk
Wireless freedom for a clean desk
products.idealFor: Small-handed buyers who want a documented angle cheaply.
products.skipIf: You want full specs before you buy.

products.name: Attoe Gaming Mouse with 5D Rocker, Wireless Vertical Mouse with 2400 DPI
products.verdict: An odd one out: a wireless vertical mouse with a 5D rocker and gaming-style DPI.
products.description:
The Attoe is a cordless upright mouse that mixes office ergonomics with a gamer-style 2400 DPI sensor, and it adds a 5D rocker for extra inputs. Expect it in the $25 to $50 bucket.

It ranks last because the listing carries a small review sample and a gaming-first pitch that does not fit every office. The 5D rocker adds inputs you can map to scrolling or shortcuts, which some people will enjoy. It is the only mouse here pitching itself to casual gamers.

It works for someone who wants one wireless mouse for office tasks and relaxed gaming. For pure ergonomics, the Lift or Lekvey are safer.
pros: 5D rocker adds extra shortcut inputs
2400 DPI covers casual gaming
Mid-budget price for a hybrid design
Wireless link frees the desk
cons: Few owner opinions to lean on
Gaming focus is wasted in offices
products.idealFor: Casual gamers who also work at the same desk.
products.skipIf: You want a proven ergonomic office mouse.

methodology.title: Wireless link quality
methodology.description: We favored mice with a dongle, Bluetooth or both and checked whether each listing says how many devices can pair.

methodology.title: Battery convenience
methodology.description: Rechargeable cells scored above AA designs for daily ease, while the spec sheet decided how clearly each battery type is documented.

methodology.title: Hand fit and tilt
methodology.description: Body size and any stated tilt angle were weighed against typical hand sizes, since fit decides whether people keep a vertical mouse.

methodology.title: Buttons and software
methodology.description: Programmable buttons, DPI options and companion software earned credit when they add real shortcuts, not just a longer feature list.

methodology.title: Value and owner confidence
methodology.description: Each pick was judged within its price bucket, with a smaller body of owner feedback lowering a score slightly.

whatMatters.detail: A 2.4GHz dongle plugs into a USB port and usually wakes quickly, but it occupies the port and only works with that one computer. Bluetooth uses the radio built into the machine, so it leaves the port free and can switch between devices. Look for the words dual mode or Bluetooth in the title, and check that your computer has the port the dongle needs.

AA battery mice are cheap and let you swap in a fresh cell instantly, but they add weight and a recurring cost. Rechargeable models skip the swap and stay lighter, yet need a charge cycle and a USB cable. Check the listing for the phrase built-in rechargeable and for whether the mouse works while charging.

A mouse that stores several pairings lets you switch between a work laptop and a personal tablet with one button. A single-device mouse is simpler and cheaper but locks you to one machine. If you use more than one computer, pay for multi-device support; if you do not, skip it.

Wireless vertical mice vary a lot in size, and a full-size shell can feel like a tent over a small hand. Compact bodies fit smaller palms and travel better. Compare the stated hand size or look for reviews that mention hand length before choosing.

Extra thumb buttons can run shortcuts such as copy, paste and undo, which saves clicks in repetitive work. They usually need the maker's software to configure, and some do not remember settings across computers. Check whether the mouse stores profiles on board before relying on custom maps.

howToChoose.intro: Start with how many computers the mouse needs to serve, since the link type follows from that.

cards.label: Dongle
cards.text: Plug-and-play with a steady link for one computer, at the cost of a USB port. The Anker, Lekvey and ProtoArc use this approach.

cards.label: Bluetooth
cards.text: Frees the port and pairs with tablets and extra laptops. The Logitech MX Vertical and Lift offer it alongside a dongle.

howToChoose.note: Choose the dual-mode Logitech if you use more than one device.

howToChoose.subheading: For Travel and Laptop Bags Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A compact body, Bluetooth so you do not lose a dongle, and a rechargeable battery that spares you a spare cell.

cards.label: In this ranking
cards.text: The Logitech Lift is the best fit for a bag, and the ProtoArc is the cheaper compact choice if you accept a dongle.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You use more than one computer or need shortcut buttons. The Logitech MX Vertical and Razer Pro Click V2 earn their premium.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You work from one desk. The Lekvey covers the basics for very little.

faq.a: Dongle connections are usually responsive enough for office work, and Bluetooth is fine for typical tasks. Gaming is a different case, and the Attoe is the only pick here aimed at it, so competitive players should look at dedicated gaming mice.

faq.q: What is the usual mistake when buying a wireless vertical mouse?
faq.a: Assuming every wireless model includes Bluetooth. Several of the budget picks use only a dongle, so a tablet or phone cannot pair. Read the connection line carefully before buying.

faq.q: Is a rechargeable model worth it over AA?
faq.a: For daily use, yes. You avoid the running cost and the dead-battery surprise, and the mouse stays lighter. A charge cycle every few weeks is a small price, and the AA Anker only wins if you hate cables.

faq.q: How do I set up a dual-mode Logitech?
faq.a: Plug in the receiver for dongle mode, or hold the connect button to pair over Bluetooth. Logitech's software then lets you store more devices and set up buttons, though basic pointing works without it.

faq.q: How should I look after the battery?
faq.a: Charge before it fully drains, avoid leaving it in a hot car and switch the mouse off when travelling. Lithium cells wear faster in heat, so storage temperature matters more than usage.

faq.q: Will a dongle mouse work on a laptop with only USB-C?
faq.a: Only with an adapter. The dongle models here use USB-A receivers, so a USB-C-only laptop needs a small adapter or a Bluetooth model like the Logitech Lift.

finalTake: The Logitech MX Vertical remains the best all-round wireless vertical mouse thanks to its dual link, rechargeable battery and multi-device pairing. If your hand is small or this is your first vertical mouse, the Lift is the smarter buy. On a tight budget, the Lekvey gives you a rechargeable dongle mouse for very little, and the Razer is the choice for button-heavy workflows.
